text:
Abraham is bidden to take his son, his only son, whom he loves; and of what Abraham feels we are told nothing. The question raised by the episode is left unanswered from first to last. We are never admitted into his mind. He makes no protest; he does not bargain; he is less a character here than a silence, and in that silence lies the whole meaning of the episode. He is no longer the man who pleaded with God for Sodom.

The three days of travel may be read as a kind of suspended sentence: outwardly nothing happens; inwardly everything. We hear of the servants, the wood, the knife, and the fire, and so the instruments of the act are named before the act itself. Obedience and horror are kept side by side, and neither is suffered to prevail over the other. Faith, in this story, is no feeling; it is rather a kind of geometry, measured out in the wood, the knife, and the fire.

Isaac is the child of the covenant, through whom the nations are to be blessed; and the promise is now turned into a test. Laid beside the earlier promise, the difference between the two grows narrower than we should expect. Everything turns on one word, _hineni_, "here I am," which Abraham speaks three times: to God, to Isaac, to the angel. Each time it means something different; each time it costs him more; and to declare himself present is, for Abraham, to declare what he is about to lose.

What Isaac knows we are not told. He carries the wood; he asks about the lamb; he receives an answer which is no answer. Of his thoughts there is nothing, only that they went, both of them, together. The phrase recurs, as though repetition might stand in for explanation. The question of his consent is raised and quietly set down again; obedience, strictly reckoned, leaves nothing over.

A reader who attends to what is missing will be rewarded. Sarah has no place in the chapter, and her death is announced in the very next verse. Without stating it, the scene suggests that something in the household did not survive the mountain. The meaning lies partly in what is omitted, and the silence is a kind of testimony, more than a mere want of speech. Abraham returns to the servants; of Isaac there is no mention, and the story turns away at the moment when a lesser story would linger.

It may be objected that this reticence belongs simply to the economy of ancient narrative, which rarely reports feeling and never explains; and in some sense the objection may be true. Yet elsewhere the same narrator tells us plainly what men feel: Esau cries out, Jacob is afraid, Joseph weeps. The reticence here is deliberate and not accidental. In this voice restraint becomes a kind of accusation, and we feel it most when we remember Joseph weeping.

Between the God who promises and the God who demands, no settlement is reached; the writer keeps both before us and declines to choose. The question is unanswerable, and its unanswerableness is itself the answer; to read the chapter is to be tried by it. Abraham stands on the mountain with the knife raised, the ram not yet seen; and there the reader is left with him.

Genesis 22 is less a story of sacrifice than a story of reading; it teaches that the things of most importance are those a text declines to say. What it withholds is what it gives. The brevity of the chapter is the reader's burden, and each gap lays a demand upon us: Abraham's silence, Isaac's question, Sarah's absence, the narrator's refusal to explain.
